Perennialists argue that themes which 'developed independent of contact between the cultures concerned' likely point to deeper truths. Critics answer that perennialism is ahistorical, overemphasises similarities and downplays differences, and (Craig Martin) makes unfalsifiable claims resembling the 'no true Scotsman' fallacy.

wording: P83 surveyed 464 regular chanters from 33 countries with the MEQ30: 60% met the criterion for a complete mystical experience (over 60% on all four factors), and neither the chi-square test of tradition (chi2(8) = 12.573, p = 0.127) nor a one-way ANOVA across nine traditions (F(8,392) = 1.367, p = 0.209) found a difference by tradition, although subscale profiles differed (interaction F(24,1176) = 1.828, p = 0.009). Taketina, a practice not tied to a belief system, had the highest proportion of complete mystical experiences, which P83 calls surprising; P83 presents the features that may promote mystical experience during chanting as a convergence of factors.

counterevidence_limits: Self-selected, mostly Australian and US, 75% female sample; cross-sectional self-report with an instrument whose perennialist origin P84 criticises; tradition groups were small (5-23%).

wording: Instrument toy for P84's critique: nine traditions, six experience dimensions, an instrument that measures three. When traditions differ only on the three unmeasured dimensions, the instrument finds a difference in 5% of 300 studies (its false-positive rate) while the unmeasured dimensions differ in 100%; with no differences anywhere the rates are 3% and 6%. A null result on a common-core instrument such as P83's is therefore compatible with traditions that differ on what the instrument does not measure.
confidence: Low as a model of religious experience (toy)
counterevidence_limits: Toy; dimensions, effect size (0.5) and sample sizes are the agent's; it shows a logical possibility, not that traditions differ.
operationalization: PHI Convergence = common core vs instrument scope
